title: Breaks
subtitle: A few seconds of drums that became the raw material of new music
intro: A break is the moment in a record when everything drops out except the drums. Follow a few of those moments from Bronx parties to Compton to London, as the break goes from a DJ technique to a sampled loop to a rhythm chopped up and put back in a new order, and turns into the raw material of new music. One of the recordings belonged to a man who was never paid for any of its uses.

steps.framing: Start in the Bronx in 1973. Kool Herc noticed that dancers went wild when a funk record dropped down to just the drums. That breakdown was recorded to lift a live crowd, and James Brown's band had recorded one of the best of them. Herc heard it as something to repeat.

Herc played breaks from two copies of a record, switching between them, so the drums kept going as long as the dancers wanted. The Incredible Bongo Band's 'Apache' had a long bongo and drum section. It did not sell when it came out, but it became one of the first great hip-hop records through DJs playing it, not through sampling. The break as a piece of music came before the technology to capture it.

Herc found the break by eye, so the joins were rough. Grandmaster Flash cued the second copy on headphones and dropped it in exactly on the beat, which turned a party trick into a technique anyone could learn. He refined it rather than inventing it: the break as the unit is Herc's, and the clean loop, which is what makes it something to build with, is Flash's.

Fifteen years after Herc, the break is sampled rather than played from two records. N.W.A built 'Straight Outta Compton' on six seconds of drums that Gregory Coleman of the Winstons played in 1969, the first sampled use of the Amen break on the map. Richard Spencer, who owned the song's rights, was never paid for this or any later use, and that belongs to the story as much as the sound does.

In Britain the same six seconds were chopped up, sped up and retimed until they were barely recognisable. Shy FX's 'Original Nuttah' in 1994 was built on the Amen break and reached the British singles chart. One recording became the basis of a whole genre two decades and an ocean away from where it started.

outro: The break started as a trick at Bronx parties and ended up as the base of whole kinds of music. Each stop kept the last stop's material and changed what was done with it: repeat it, loop it cleanly, sample it, chop it. On the Amen break's stop, try the demo to hear the difference between looping a break and chopping it.
